protections: Every XML entity decoder must obtain its parser from a SAXParserFactory that refuses external DTD/DOCTYPE resolution, external general and parameter entities, and XInclude; at the pinned commit the only factory is a bare SAXParserFactory.newInstance with no features set (scala-xml/src/main/scala/org/http4s/scalaxml/package.scala:22), reached by the implicit xmlDecoder (ElemInstances.scala:86) and by the deprecated, non-implicit xml[F] (ElemInstances.scala:65).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The parallel entry is @deprecated("Blocks. Use xmlDecoder with an Async constraint.", "0.23.12") (ElemInstances.scala:56), is not implicit, and is never referenced by the pinned test suite, so a solver can argue it is a superseded legacy path outside the advisory's scope.

saxFactory is an abstract protected member of the public ElemInstances trait (ElemInstances.scala:38) that the package object merely overrides (package.scala:21-22); a caller that supplies its own factory owns its configuration, so only the package-object default needs hardening.

The trait already carries two decoders for the same Elem sink (ElemInstances.scala:57 and :76); a NodeSeq/Document codec written with XML.loadString or XML.withSAXParser would look like an ordinary convenience addition, and XML.loadString is scala-xml's idiomatic one-liner.
Validating XML against a DTD is a real consumer need, so an xmlValidatingDecoder that deliberately re-enables DTD/DOCTYPE processing is a defensible feature rather than a security regression.

conflicts.what: The blunt fix for T1, disallow-doctype-decl=true, rejects documents that carry an internal DTD subset (e.g. <!DOCTYPE greeting [<!ENTITY who 'world'>]><greeting>&who;</greeting>), which parse today through ElemInstances.scala:66 / :87 and would surface as a 400 via ElemInstances.scala:68-69 / :90-91; only the narrower load-external-dtd=false plus external-general-entities=false plus external-parameter-entities=false keeps T6 working.

The fix that closes T3 (apply the hardening inside the trait over whatever factory saxFactory returns, or make the member non-overridable) leaves the package-object val itself unconfigured (package.scala:22); if the hidden test inspects the exposed saxFactory's features rather than only submitting XXE bodies, the T3-shaped fix fails the T1 check and vice versa.

A validating decoder needs DOCTYPE/DTD processing that T6 also demands, but T5 relaxes the guard deliberately for that consumer, so a shared hardening helper must distinguish internal-subset parsing from external resolution rather than gate on the DOCTYPE at all.

fairness_risks: Documents that legitimately carry an internal DTD subset parse today (ElemInstances.scala:66 and :87) and a blanket disallow-doctype-decl=true turns them into 400 MalformedMessageBodyFailure; a security rule that rejects every DOCTYPE contradicts this working behaviour.

Any SAXParseException is already mapped to a 400 (ElemInstances.scala:68-69 and :90-91), so a hardened parser's rejection of a DOCTYPE is indistinguishable to the client from malformed XML, and a fix that raises a different exception type (e.g. an IOException from a failed external fetch) escapes the recover clause at ElemInstances.scala:90 and becomes a 500.

The hardened configuration lives on a single shared mutable val (package.scala:22) used concurrently by the parallel-decode test (ScalaXmlSuite.scala:70-82); a fix that sets features per request rather than once at construction races.
Both decoders accept MediaType.text.html (ElemInstances.scala:59 and :78), so refusing DOCTYPEs on the HTML media type may reject legitimate HTML-ish XML bodies.

Legitimate XInclude and external-DTD-backed validation are refused by the required rule; XInclude is off by default in JAXP, so a client relying on the JDK default already sees no XInclude, but a client relying on external DTD resolution does lose behaviour.

design.why: The strongest available design is T1 (the shared factory default, M4, no reason to dismiss) plus T3 (the abstract protected saxFactory on the public trait, M5, dismissible as 'your own factory is your own responsibility') as the two places that really exist at the pinned commit, with T4 (a NodeSeq/Document codec written against XML.loadString or XML.withSAXParser, M2, mimo-type) and T5 (a validating decoder that deliberately re-enables DTD processing, M2, mimo-type) planted in the two injection-room slots at ElemInstances.scala:76 and :57. T2 (deprecated xml[F], M1) is the deepseek-type miss but it is closed by T1's own factory guard, and T6 (internal DTD subset must keep working, M11) is the mimo-type coupled value that dictates the granularity of T1's fix, so both ride on T1's group rather than adding independence. That design has four groups with four different dismissals and covers both model types, and it beats an all-in-the-factory design because only T3 and T4 survive a solver who hardens package.scala:22 correctly. It is still thin: the checkout itself supplies exactly one independent real group, the whole library is two source files (ElemInstances.scala and package.scala), the pinned suite has no DOCTYPE/XXE test of any kind, and T4 and T5 do not exist in the tree and must be written by the task author.
